Messages.Author: Matthew Heslin
Messages.Body:
Hey all,

I wasn't sure if Eric Simon would post a report on
this event, as it was his baby, and I just volunteered to
judge so he wouldn't have to coordinate and judge
both a Regional Qualifier and a local event.

Seventeen Methuselahs turned up at the Fight Shop
in Chicago to duke it out for the Now Legendary
Meaty Sandwich Challenge. Mike Ooi has made this
Sandwich available to any out-of-state player who can
conquer the local talent, but thus far none have been
able to take it from Illinois' borders.

Wes Weston stayed through the weekend to
earn the "longest distance traveled" award, and suffered
much stealth-bleedery and crap deals (Hi Halcyan!).
Indiana's Lafayette group turned out in force, such that
I had to re-seat players in one round to avoid an all-
Indiana table. My apologies to Tim, who had to sit
at the mostly-Indiana table when it was not conducive
to his deck's style.

Two rounds gave us five finalists, though things
were tight enough to almost require a coin flip to get
the fifth and sixth place finalists. Chicago favorite
Boris Zaretsky went into the final in first place, followed
by a tie for second between Cameron Domer and
Ahmed I-Am-Not-Going-To-Attempt-To-Spell [Habbiyyeh].
Cameron won a coin toss to nose ahead of Ahmed.
Megan Bailey from Lafayette and Rick Irvine from...
Lafayette?... filled out the last spots. (Eric, feel free
to correct this as necessary.)

Seating in the final looked like this:

Boris, with first transfer and an Animalism weenie
deck, bleeding into-
Cameron, with a power stealth bleed OBT/DOM
deck, bleeding into-
Rick, with a Malkavian Group 1-2 deck, bleeding
into-
Megan, with a Black Hand AUS/OBF deck,
bleeding into-
Ahmed, with a Tremere/!Tremere intercept and
Burst of Sunlight deck, bleeding Boris.

Boris showed the table what an opening turn
was, with a Powerbase: Montreal and Lisa Noble.
Rick turned over an Ohanna on his first turn, and
Megan a Piotr Andreikov. Ahmed showed Selena
for his first vampire, and Cameron showed... Aurora
Van Brande, Paladin? It looked like Cameron had
switched decks between rounds, since he was more
likely to show Gratiano, Lucita, or some other scary
bleed monster.
Boris brought out Christianus Lionel, Nigel the
Shunned, geared up with Raven Spies and recruited
Gregory Winter. Megan pulled out Marijava Thuggees,
which cemented her for "Most Interesting Deck in
the final" in my ballot. Rick started his offense with
minor stealth bleeds for 1, and showed Roland Bishop
and Normal. Cameron's second vampire was Lucita
(adv.), which was more in line with his history.
Rick used skill cards to make his Malk midgets
more menacing - he started to throw Govern bleeds
at Megan with Ohanna, and bleeds for 1 with Normal
and Roland. He also brought out Mariel, Lady Thunder.
Boris's building spree continued unabated, with
Sandra White and Bobby Lemon appearing, and all
his minions getting more and more gear. The first
noteworthy combats started, with Ahmed throwing
agg damage at Boris's ANI minions, and the ANI
minions hitting back for Carrion Crows and Aid from
Bats for 3 damage. Both were usually able to come
back from these combats, though Ahmed's minions
were depleted of blood much more quickly.
Megan pulled Teresita and Ahmed pulled Bryan
Van Duesen, which brought Megan slightly low on
pool -- Ahmed's pool was mostly healthy because
Megan was dealing with Rick's increasingly dangerous
offense. Cameron's bleeds are hitting him reliably at
this point, but Cameron is keeping his bleeds at a
survivable level here, 1-3. All that changes when
Cameron smells weakness and lunges at Rick --
Aurora hits with a Govern bleed for 3, stealthed to
it's destination, and Lucita mixes up a Govern bleed
with a Foreshadowing Destruction for 6. Rick's
first ousted at 0:37.
Megan promptly responds with Thuggee (D)
actions to deal 1 damage to Aurora, twice, which
puts the Paladin in the dirt. Ahmed tries to put some
hurt on Boris, since Megan looks well-occupied with
Cameron, but ends up with Bryan and Muaziz put in
torpor from fighting Boris's ANI horde. Bryan gets
himself out with a Recure of the Homeland (so good),
and Muaziz gets rescued by Lucita on Cameron's next
turn. Cameron's looking for a little cooperation at this
point to avoid being the scariest thing on the table.
Boris has already sent Gregory Winter to clean up
after Aurora (Gregory - so good), so Cameron has
to bring up Julia Prima to back up the Girl from Aragon.
Megan deals with some of her pool issues with twin
Reunion Kamuts by Teresita and Piotr, and puts more
pressure on Ahmed by using her Thuggee to ping
Muaziz, which puts her in the dirt as well.
Boris looks like he's running the show now, by
keeping minor bleed pressure on Cameron and
keeping Ahmed at arm's length, blocking- and
combat-wise. Cameron's first attempt at Megan
gets bounced in to Ahmed for 3 pool loss, which
reins him in for a turn. Megan smells a lack of block
and Deflections, and bleeds for a total of 5 on her
turn. Ahmed plays a Blood Doll on his remaining
conscious minion and gulps.
Cameron, aware that his presence in this game
could be quickly obviated, thinks real real hard and
goes for Megan's throat. Lucita throws a bleed for
1, plays Seduction, Shadow Play, Command of the
Beast and Conditioning to get it in -- and Julia throws
a Tenebrous Form, Shadow Play, Conditioning
bleed for the kill. Megan ousted at 1:01.
Ahmed blinks a few times and says, "done."
Boris keeps doing what he's doing - hunting for
pool gain, rescuing minions in torpor, stealing blood
with Gregory Winter, and tossing little bleeds at his
prey. However, he also rescues Ahmed's minions
to keep him in the game against Cameron's bleed
machine.
Cameron's bleeds are all successfully blocked
by Selena and Bryan, though they keep going back
to torpor. Cameron adds Banjoko to his line-up
for added bleeding power.
Ahmed, on his turn, is offered a deal for a 2-2-1
split: Boris gets 2, Cameron gets no more than the
2 he's already taken, and Ahmed gets 1. This looks
pretty frickin' sweet for him, and he accepts. Boris
then rescues all of Ahmed's folks. Cameron's next
turn is blocked bleeds and Deflected bleeds, and
his shiny new Banjoko ends up eating gravedirt.
Ahmed hunts with his empty vampires, Boris's turn
is a brief whirlwind of Army of Rats, Gregory Winter
stealing blood, and bleeds for 1, adding up to Cameron
getting ousted at 1:37. Mutual withdrawal sets up the
end results of:

Boris, 2 VP
Cameron, 2 VP
Ahmed, 1 VP
Megan, 0 VP
Rick, 0 VP

No real rules questions came up, so my job was
easy. Thanks to Eric Simon for doing all the real
work, and for having FreeCell on his laptop. : )
Thanks to everyone who came, and I hope we'll see
you in Milwaukee for the May Day tournament!

--heslin, self-hypemeister

1 VP might not necessarily be better than 0 VP's, depending on your seeding. If
you have the highest seed, it's better for you to get 0 VP's and let someone
sweep (giving you 2nd place) than to be on the 1 VP end of a 2-2-1 split
(leaving you at only 3rd place).

Halcyan 2

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Halcyan 2 wrote:
> 1 VP might not necessarily be better than 0 VP's, depending on your seeding. If
> you have the highest seed, it's better for you to get 0 VP's and let someone
> sweep (giving you 2nd place) than to be on the 1 VP end of a 2-2-1 split
> (leaving you at only 3rd place).

A pathological example, to be sure, but to clear it away:

1 VP is necessarily better than 0 VP's under the "play to win" rule.

A four-way tie for 2nd at 0VP is lower on the win chart than a third
place 1VP finish.

Play to win: get the win if you can. If you can't, get as many VPs
as you can (which, when observed, leads to the conclusion in the
previous paragraph).

--

> Notice that nowhere is anything said about placement. Overall
> placement is technically an outside consideration. 1VP is better than
> 0, so "placing third" is actually better than "placing second" in the

Placement is the highest priority, actually. It just turns out that
in a preliminary round, tied for second with 0 VPs (really 3.5th
place) is worse than third with 1 VP. In a final round where you're
winning tiebreaks, it is better to come in sole 2nd place with 0 VPs,
as LSJ clarified above.

LSJ, one more question: is it sportsmanlike to prevent someone else
from getting the game win, at the expense of higher placement? As an
example:

4 player game, A -> B -> C -> D. D was ousted. Then C was ousted.
B's library is exhausted, there's 1 minute left in the round, A cannot
possibly oust B, nor can B possibly oust A. Would it be
unsportsmanlike for A to prevent B from withdrawing? A benefits from
the withdraw, because he would go from 3rd place to tied for 2nd
place, but B would get the Game Win.

By my current definition of "sportsmanlike conduct", I would have no
problem with A preventing B from getting the Game Win, but maybe
that's an incorrect definition.

Thank you, as always!

Ira

Well, you all have a problem, then. This is unenforceable and WILL be
broken every time the situation comes up.

It is also impossible to detect. In the recent tournament in Charlotte,
I gained 2 quick VPs and then, after several turns of flailing around
trying to make further progress, deliberately allowed myself to be bled
out from 4 pool with a Wake and Deflection in hand.

It was clear at the time that I would not be able to oust my prey, and
that he would surely be able to oust my predator and then myself. I,
therefore, with 2VP in hand and a possible Game Win, deliberately set up
a situation where the best possible result would be 2-2-1 with no Game
Win, instead of 2-3 and a Game Win going to someone else. (There was a
third possibility, that of the table timing out and me getting the GW
with 2-1.5-0.5, but that was VERY unlikely).

Now, interestingly enough, this example doesn't violate the "play to
win" paradigm, because I was attempting to lock in a tie for 1st. But
it DOES demonstrate that there is no possible way to detect or enforce
that paradigm against someone who chooses to let themselves lose for
external reasons, instead of attempting to defend to the bitter end. I
don't have to show my hand to anyone; all I have to say is "no block,
how much?" and let them play the Conditioning.

Losing to ensure someone else's sweep will work exactly the same way.

-- Derek

> Again, since placement is not part of the "play to win" paradigm, it
> is an outside consideration, and it is therefore unsportsmanlike to
> choose it over maximizing VPs.

not in the finals. In the finals, you're playing for your place in
the tournement directly, thus if you are about to be ousted, it is in
your best interest to help the ousting deck sweep. See LSJ's last
response in this thread for more info. It basically says that, with a
set tiebreaker, if you can't get first, and get second if the person
who's getting first sweeps, but third if you make this other deal that
nets you a VP, playing to "win" is playing for second. How you get
there is up to you.

Similarly (IIRC and IANLSJ) I think that prize support from the finals
*IS* a valid consideration when making deals in the finals, although
I'm not really clear on that.

Also, once you've got first place in the finals you can do whatever
you want to do with the rest of the vps (ie it's: you 2vp (to seed)
1vp to your first prey (ousted) you can transfer yourself out, getting
first place, and go catch your plane.)

Cameron

PoMadison

Messages.Author: Ira
Messages.Body:
Hey Eric,

> Where are you getting that?

LSJ's previous message, in this very thread. Here is the relevant
quote:

> > Therefore, it seems to me that in a final game, the most sportsmanlike
> > thing to do would be to play for second place (assuming I can't get
> > first) instead of getting more VPs but placing worse.
>
> Yes. Second (alone) is better than 3rd (alone).

Of course, there are several key assumptions there, including:

- It is a final game
- You are winning tie-breaks
- You have no reasonable chance at 1st place

> That's what "play to win" has ALWAYS meant, every time LSJ has ever
> clarified it.

Remember that the actual rule is "behave in a respectful and
sportsmanlike manner at all times." (Tournament Rule 2.3.) That
includes more than just "play to win."

> Placement has absolutely nothing to do with it.

That's actually incorrect. Placement is everything. It just happens
that in a preliminary round, more VPs always means higher placement
(or at least no worse placement) since there are no tie-breakers. In
a final round, where there are tie-breakers, sometimes it's possible
to get less VPs and a higher placement, which is good sportsmanship.

> > LSJ, one more question: is it sportsmanlike to prevent someone else
> > from getting the game win, at the expense of higher placement? As an
> > example:
>
> Again, since placement is not part of the "play to win" paradigm, it
> is an outside consideration, and it is therefore unsportsmanlike to
> choose it over maximizing VPs.

While you may be right, you are starting from "play to win" and
deducing from there. That is incorrect. For tournament play, you
should start from "behave in a sportsmanlike manner" and deduce from
there. Play to win is certainly part of being a good sport, though.

At his convenience, I'd like an official LSJ answer regarding the
situation I posed previously in this thread. The general situation
is:

- Prelim round
- No reasonable chance at a game win
- I have the opportunity to gain some VPs (and improve my placement)
and allow someone else to gain the GW, OR decline to gain some VPs and
prevent someone from getting the GW.

Regarding Derek's comment that the rule is unenforceable, I generally
agree. Nonetheless, there are many players (myself included) who
voluntarily choose to play by the correct rules, and therefore I'm
asking these questions so that I can be enlightened. While I
certainly could bend the rules without getting caught, it's my
intention to understand the rules and then play by them.

Also, if a Judge clearly and politely communicates the rules to a
player, many players will choose to act in accordance with those rules
even if the player could break the rules without getting caught.

Ira

> > thing to do would be to play for second place (assuming I can't get
> > first) instead of getting more VPs but placing worse.
>
> Yes. Second (alone) is better than 3rd (alone).

#1 and #2 seem contradictory to me. In the second statement, you
make it clear that in the final (if you're winning tiebreaks) it's
better to get 0 VPs and come in 2nd (alone) than 1 VP and come in 3rd
(alone).

> As has already been covered, finalists can be assumed to be playing
> to win, so the question of priority doesn't arise.

Regardless of what we *assume* the finalists are doing, the
tournament rules actually *obligate* them to "behave in a
sportsmanlike manner at all times." For the final, does that
obligation mean:

a) They must play to place first, and if they can't, they can do
whatever they want.
b) They must play to place first, and if not, maximize VPs.
(contradicted by #2 above)
c) They must play to place first, and if not, maximize placement
(contradicted by #1 above)
d) They can play however they want (this doesn't seem sportsmanlike to
me.)
e) Something else that I didn't list.

> Moot, since there would never be a case where this would provide
> any meaningful benefit to A.

A may gain significant benefit and pleasure from preventing his prey
from getting a Game Win. It certainly isn't a moot question for me; a
similar situation arose in my most recent game. "If I can't win, no
one can win."

> But sure. And then, as with any
> violation of any rule, the judge can set it aright.

OK.

Thanks for your seemingly limitless patience! I personally really
appreciate all the time you spend answering my silly/stupid questions
about this awesome game.

Thank you!

Ira

Hey LSJ,

> #1 is for preliminary rounds. #2 cannot apply to preliminary rounds.
> Therefore the contradiction is avoided.

Ah! I understand now. Thank you!

> f) They play to win by default, since there are no further games
> to consider as out-of-game considerations.

I understand what we assume by default. I'm asking what the rules
actually require of them.

For instance, as a finalist, if I wanted to oust myself from the
beginning of the game simply to prove this assumption wrong, I would
be probihited from doing so by the good sportsmanship rules. Any
reasonable judge would stop me from ousting myself.

Finalists are actually *obligated* to play in a certain way
(regardless of what we assume), and I'm asking you to tell me what
that obligation is for the final game. Consider this case:

In a final round, I'm in a pretty bad situation, but I still have a
reasonable chance to win. If I try for the win, I'll either win or
come in 5th place. In a non-final game, I would be prohibited from
making a table split deal at this point because I still have a
reasonable chance to win. In the final game, am I free to make a
table split deal (3-2, with me getting the 2) even though I have a
reasonable chance at the win? As a player, maybe I prefer a very good
chance at 2nd place, instead of a small chance at first and a high
chance of 5th.

Furthermore, I realize that these rules are nearly impossible for a
Judge to enforce. I want to understand the rules so that I can
voluntarily follow them, and I'm sure many other players would too.

Thanks again,

Ira

Hey LSJ,

This is going to be my last post on this point for a while; your
patience with me is super-human, and I really appreciate it!

> The "play to win" rule requires nothing of them, since they abide

win even if he is obviously not playing to win.

being required to follow the normal definition of the sportsmanship

a final. I think most judges are very respectful of the final; a
general requirement of play to win seems good to me, mostly to prevent
early table split deals.

But then logic would dictate that a player would never oust himself at the
beggining of the game in a preliminary round either, so you wouldn't need
the PTW to apply to the preliminary rounds either (at least for that case).
Yet, some people will do it.
Maybe they're pissed at their gran-predator. Maybe they have to catch a
train. Maybe they have a particular dislike for his predator's minions and
don't want to play against them. Maybe they're just plain crazy.

Any of those reasons could apply equally to the final game, so I see no
reason to drop the rule for the finals. There may be fewer situations where
the rule is necessary, but it's still necessary.

But there are reasons why you would oust yourself at the beginning of
the game in a preliminary round. For instance, you swept round 1 and
2, so you now have 2 TW and 10 VP. With the number of players in the
tournament you are very confident about making the finals as is. In
round three you could oust yourself at the beginning of the game in
order to either help someone else into the finals or help keep someone
out of the finals. If it is the final round there is no advantage to
ousting yourself. You could oust yourself because of collusion or
accepting a bribe, by LSJ has already pointed out that this is also
illegal/unsportsmanlike play.
